articles.text: Editor: The Post’s coverage in narrative and photographs of this year’s 4th of July Parade was quite extensive! Descriptions of the holiday’s events appeared on 8 pages, and I counted 60 photos. Imagine my surprise and disappointment, therefore, not to find any reference in all of this parade coverage to the participation of the Piedmont Community Band, which has played in the parade for 38 years. The only reference at all (that I almost missed) was to those who may “join the Piedmont marching band” on page 20 in the article about American music. The Post’s articles about the parade mentioned over 25 entries, including music provided by the Barrelhouse Jazz Band (1 photo), the Zenith Parade Band (2 photos), and the California Percussionists (3 photos), and there was 1 photo of the Cub Scout Kazoo Band. I don’t begrudge any of those entries the coverage they got; I think it’s great. But there was nothing about the homegrown Piedmont Community Band; Jane Reed, its Founder and Coordinator of 38 years; Ken Kawaichi, it’s band leader of 36 years; Elaine Lindenmayer, its majorette who at age 70 twirled for her 35th time; or its dedicated musicians, many of whom dust off their instruments annually just to delight parade-goers with their perky drum cadences and marching music. I admit my bias, since the band’s majorette is my mom, but I know that much of our Piedmont community looks forward annually to our local band’s appearance. Indeed, the Piedmont Community Band is a Piedmont treasure. The Post no doubt played a part in the band’s performance this year by dedicating space to calls for musicians, and in the past, the Post has duly recognized the Piedmont Community Band. Perhaps this year was an aberration. I hope the Post will give it due recognition in the future. Thank you for considering my thoughts. Evan Lindenmayer
articles.title: Piedmont Community Band

articles.text: As I write it is Wednesday of Vacation Bible Camp week at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church. I am sure that those most directly involved in the camp are very tired, wondering if they can summon the energy for two more days while the campers are wishing that there were two more weeks of camp instead of two more days. VBC is a most impressive effort, one that shapes all those involved. For the adults it is an opportunity to connect directly with the kids. For the youth leaders it is a valuable opportunity to grow as teacher, mentor, organizer and leader. For the campers it is an invitation to learn the stories of the Bible and learn to think theologically about their lives and the world around them. In this year’s camp the Bible stories on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday focused on Joseph of Egypt. On Thursday, Jesus of Nazareth, particularly his passion, was the focus. There are important parallels between Joseph and Jesus. These have long been noted by Christian theologians, leachers and leaders. Their names are similar. Joseph means “God gives increase.” Jesus means “God saves.” Both experienced family conflict. Both “went down” to Egypt. Both knew rejection. Both knew suffering, Joseph was imprisoned in a cistern. Jesus was buried in a tomb. Joseph saved his people from famine. Jesus saved his people for a ministry of love. The five Bible points from this year’s camp pertain to both Joseph and Jesus and provide the basis for a healthy theology as well as healthy theological reflection. • God loves you no matter what. (In the midst of family tension, it was important for Jesus and Joseph to remember this.) • God is with you everywhere. (This was true for Joseph when he was in prison and for Jesus when he was being tempted in the wilderness.) • God is in charge. (Even when, like Joseph, you are entrusted with helping a country survive a famine and, like Jesus, you need to feed 5,000 with five loaves and two fish.) • God is stronger than anything. (The cold cistern and the quiet tomb included.)
articles.title: Good Theology

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will discuss Laboratories of Autocracy: A Wake-Up Call from Behind the Lines by David Pepper at its upcoming book meeting on August 16. Pepper’s Laboratories shows the “high profile antics of national politics,” and spotlights what can often be corruption in statehouses across the nation, which the author asserts pose the greatest threat to American democracy. The book outlines 30 steps that need to be taken, from federal action to individual steps, that help every citizen fight back against corruption in their own communities. Pepper is a writer, lawyer, former elected official, and served as the Chairman of the Ohio Democratic Party between 2015 and 2021. articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved on July 18 an agreement with ELS Architecture and Design (ELS) for frontage and right-of-way improvements for the proposed municipal pool. “Our project management team, led by George Sanen [of Griffin Architecture] has been keenly aware of grabbing opportunities to save time and money, as well as to mitigate risk, all three of which are in play here,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. ELS was awarded an agreement to provide design services for the new Community Pool in October 2021. The original agreement did not include rightof-way or pedestrian improvements, or Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) accessibility access ramps. Tree removal and replacement, sidewalk and curb improvements were also omitted. The improvements are necessary, explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The right-of-way is defined as the area that is behind private property – usually the sidewalk, the parking strip and/or the roadway on both sides of the street – all of which will be impacted as construction begins on the pool. “Once you have left the poolside itself, that area needs i m p r ove me nt ,” G on z a le s explained. “In the case of our project, the pool stops at the fence line. The area [beyond that] was not included in the original agreement [with ELS]. Those areas were not included, but will be impacted by this project. Looking at that, Public Works has identified this as the most beneficial time to look and contemplate how we can go about these improvements.” There are several benefits to begin improvements as soon as possible, Gonzales added, the primary benefit being cost savings. Improvements would start on Bonita Avenue at the Corey Reich Tennis Courts, go down past the existing pool, past the Recreation Building and wrap around to Hillside Avenue. Gonzales noted that not all elements may need improvements, but that there is urgency is beginning an analysis now. “The last thing we want to do is finish site improvements, and then say we can’t open yet because we will have to work on the front [entry] itself,” he said. “It would be a shame to have this gorgeous, new facility, and have to tell [visitors] that they may need to park elsewhere or not use the sidewalks,” agreed Council member Betsy Andersen. The trees that surround the pool are “less than ideal for this setting,” Gonzales said, and added that this is a good time to look at replacing them with more suitable trees. Drainage improvements from fixing curb and gutter areas will also be assessed. The total cost of the improvements are not to exceed $75,140, according to the agreement between ELS and the City. business hours.

Right-of-way improvements for new pool to begin By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont City Council approved on July 18 an agreement with ELS Architecture and Design (ELS) for frontage and right-of-way improvements for the proposed municipal pool. “Our project management team, led by George Sanen [of Griffin Architecture] has been keenly aware of grabbing opportunities to save time and money, as well as to mitigate risk, all three of which are in play here,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. ELS was awarded an agreement to provide design services for the new Community Pool in October 2021. The original agreement did not include rightof-way or pedestrian improvements, or Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) accessibility access ramps. Tree removal and replacement, sidewalk and curb improvements were also omitted. The improvements are necessary, explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The right-of-way is defined as the area that is behind private property – usually the sidewalk, the parking strip and/or the roadway on both sides of the street – all of which will be impacted as construction begins on the pool. “Once you have left the poolside itself, that area needs i m p r ove me nt ,” G on z a le s explained. “In the case of our project, the pool stops at the fence line. The area [beyond that] was not included in the original agreement [with ELS]. Those areas were not included, but will be impacted by this project. Looking at that, Public Works has identified this as the most beneficial time to look and contemplate how we can go about these improvements.” There are several benefits to begin improvements as soon as possible, Gonzales added, the primary benefit being cost savings. Improvements would start on Bonita Avenue at the Corey Reich Tennis Courts, go down past the existing pool, past the Recreation Building and wrap around to Hillside Avenue. Gonzales noted that not all elements may need improvements, but that there is urgency is beginning an analysis now. “The last thing we want to do is finish site improvements, and then say we can’t open yet because we will have to work on the front [entry] itself,” he said. “It would be a shame to have this gorgeous, new facility, and have to tell [visitors] that they may need to park elsewhere or not use the sidewalks,” agreed Council member Betsy Andersen. The trees that surround the pool are “less than ideal for this setting,” Gonzales said, and added that this is a good time to look at replacing them with more suitable trees. Drainage improvements from fixing curb and gutter areas will also be assessed. The total cost of the improvements are not to exceed $75,140, according to the agreement between ELS and the City. pages.text: Wednesday, July 20, 2022 5 Just The Way I Like It Piedmont Choir’s Ensemble goes to Europe By Larissa Edel Part 1: Denmark The weeks of June 14 through 28 this summer were some of the best weeks of my life. After two-and-a-half years of the global pandemic, the Ensemble level of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir finally embarked on its long-awaited international tour to Denmark and Germany. The flight to Frankfurt was smooth and, overflowing with excitement, few of us slept. The food on our flight wasn’t that great, but we reminded ourselves of our tour motto, No matter what we eat, we have learned to say, “It’s just the way I like it.” That motto certainly came in handy on the bus ride from Frankurt to Denmark, where it was 90 degrees (F), and the bus AC broke down. Luckily, the stunning Danish countryside gave us a nice distraction. I have never seen such pristine fields of wheat, and forests so lush, or even seen so many animals just roaming free – deer, elk, even two rabbits and a fox running in a field. Denmark struck me as extremely flat: not a single mountain or even hill was spotted the entire time we were there. As it got hotter on our four-hour bus ride, our sense of reality and time started to crumble, so we decided to start singing, because after all we were a choir. The singing was out of tune, too slow, and not sung with conviction, just delirium. But we made it through to Herning, a city in central Denmark. In Herning we stayed with families of the MidtVest Children’s Choir. When time came to be given our rooming assignments, we all had our fingers crossed hoping that we would be placed with our friends. I was with one of my good friends, so I was all set. Our homestay’s name was Julie, but her name was pronounced Ulia. We were nervous because we wanted to make a good impression and had not experienced homestays before, but we all hit it off with our host families right away. Homestaying was one of the best parts of the tour. Our hosts were the kindest, most caring, and funny people that I have met. We even learned some Danish phrases: “god morgen” is “good morning,”, “tak,” is “thank you,” and “sov godt” is “sleep tight.” Even though we had a slight language barrier, it never got in the way; we always found a way to understand each other. Leaving Julie and her family when we left for Germany was one of the harder parts of the tour. While in Denmark we visited Skovsnogen (Deep Forest Art Land), a museum but an unconventional one. It was completely outside, and all the artwork was either a sculpture or some sort of Tour chaperone group, The Delta Nu’s are pictured in Deep Forest Art Land while looking out into the field in front of them: Kailamae Sands (left), Juliane Crossland, Olive Zager, Miranda Couch, Veda Pao Ziegler, and Larissa Edel. 3D object. Our choir split up into two groups, by tour chaperone groups, and we each had a guide. My group got a lovely woman named Henrietta and the other group got one of the owners of Skovsnogen, René Schmidt, an artist who created the museum in 2009. Both groups took different paths and saw different art pieces with some overlap. articles.text: Sukanya Goswami began her tenure as the new principal of Piedmont High School, on July 1, coming most recently from Miramonte High School in Orinda, where she was Assistant Principal. Goswami sat down with the Post to talk about her career and the tasks that lie ahead in her first year as the high school’s top administrator. She takes over for Adam Littlefield, who retired after five years as PHS Principal. Goswami has 20 years of experience in secondary education. She taught for 14 years as an English teacher at Newark Memorial High School, including five years as the Department Chair. Her foundation as a teacher should serve her well in the new role. “As a high school teacher, it was more than just content, it was mentoring them, guiding them, and working with their families. And I really enjoy that whole-child approach, giving and guiding them towards the future,” she explained. In 2018 she moved into an administrative role as Vice Principal at Westmoor High School in Daly City, a position she held for three years until moving to Miramonte last school year. She is no stranger to different cultures; Goswami was born and raised in Calcutta, India, and started her career teaching students and families from different backgrounds,” she said. Goswami said her goal is to always keep in mind what is best for the students. “Whenever I am having a conversation (with students, parents, staff or administrators), I want to bring the discussion back to the goal: Is this really helpful for the student? That is where it starts and that’s where it ends,” she explained. Goswami’s first task is to assemble a full roster of teachers before the school year starts. In recent years, Piedmont High has started the year lacking staff in Spanish, Science and Music. “Hiring is a big focus now at this time in all school districts. We are reaching out to the community; we are reaching out to the local colleges. California is going through a big teacher shortage; all districts are struggling to fill positions and that is very real,” she said. Goswami wants to hit the ground running and knows that outreach and transparency are key. “I would like the community to know that I am a collaborative leader, and I’m a very authentic person,” Goswami said. “So, anybody should feel free to reach out to me with their comments, concerns, and feedback. articles.text: Looking for something new to do this summer? Do you enjoy gardening and want to support the community around you? Look no further than the Piedmont Community Service Crew’s (PCSC) upcoming event on Thursday, August 4th from 9:00-11:00 a.m.. PCSC will team up with Clausen House to build two large planter boxes in the backyard of their Perkins Street residential home in Oakland. The planter boxes can hold four cubic yards of soil and will be used for growing tomatoes, basil, and cilantro. To increase engagement in the project, the Clausen House residents did their own research and compiled a list of possible plants and vegetables. Clausen House is a non-profit dedicated to providing support and services to adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Founded in 1967, it has provided housing, an employment program, education support, independent living, and recreation and health services to low income and elderly residents for over 55 years. The planter boxes will provide food and increase accessibility to gardening for residents. The project also aims to improve communal teamwork, and provide a fun, engaging activity for residents right in their own backyard. Piedmont Community Service Crew is under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council and encourages teens to lead and create events and projects oriented on providing service for the community. The non-profit teen group strives to develop projects that fit the interests and talents of crew members who express the desire to take on increased ownership in what they do by actively building, repairing, and interacting with the larger community. articles.text: “One glimpse answered ages of speculation; you could see theories falling all around.” These were the words of Harvard geologist Clifford Frondel describing his first experience studying rocks brought back from the Moon by the Apollo 11 astronauts. As we celebrate the anniversary of the moon landing this July, we hear so much about the achievements of the Apollo program in terms of engineering prowess, political will, and global pride in that “giant leap” of human endeavor. But what about the science? How much did the Apollo program contribute to science? To our understanding of the origin and structure of the Moon? Or the evolution of our Solar System. Or for that matter, the evolution of the Earth? The short answer to all of these questions: A lot. Theories that didn’t hold up after Apollo Prior to the Apollo program, there were three conflicting theories about the origin of the Moon: the fission theory; the co-accretion theory; and the capture theory. The fission theory: that early in the Solar System’s formation, when the Earth was still a hot, molten blob, its rapid rotation caused a portion of its mass to separate, going into orbit around the proto-Earth and eventually becoming the Moon. The co-accretion theory: the Earth and the Moon formed separately but close together, in the same part of the pre-solar cloud of gas and dust orbiting the early Sun. The capture theory: the Earth and the Moon formed in separate regions of the Solar System but migrated together due to the gravitational evolution of planet orbits. None of these theories survived the Apollo program. Within a few years after Apollo, as scientists studied those Moon rocks and recognized their remarkable similarity to rocks on Earth, a completely new theory emerged for how the Moon formed and how it related to the Earth. The Moon was always part of us Scientists now agree that the Moon formed as the result of a collision between the early Earth and a smaller proto-planet we now call ‘Theia.’ That collision broke away a large portion of the Earth’s outer layers, which mixed with the pulverized remnants of Theia. Much of that material fell back onto the Earth, but some of it remained in orbit and eventually coalesced into the Moon. There are many such examples of the science that came out of the Apollo program, and there’s more on the way. A large percentage of the 842 pounds of Apollo lunar rocks are still sealed in vaults, not yet subject to scientific examination. There is a lot to learn about science from studying moon rocks. So next time you hear someone claim that the Apollo program was all about politics and beating the Russians, you might want to talk to a scientist. Especially one of those who has made a career out of studying lunar rocks. And who wishes we would go get more. This article was originally published in the Piedmont Post on July 21, 2021. Gerald McKeegan is an astronomer at Chabot Space and Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. You can also see them online at https://chabotspace.org/.

articles.text: Fire of Love, a documentary film by Piedmont High School alumnus Sara Dosa, class of 2000, is now playing in select theaters and streaming online. Dosa premiered her newest documentary Fire of Love at the 2022 Sundance Film Festival, where it was shown as one of five selected for the festival in the documentary category. The film was picked up for theatrical distribution by National Geographic following the premiere. The deal for Fire of Love closed in February, with National Geographic Documentary Films closing a mid-seven-figure worldwide rights contract. Dosa, who lives in the East Bay, is an Indie Spirit Award-nominated director and Peabody award-winning producer, whose film credits include Audrie & Daisy, available on at-home streaming service Netflix, The Seer and Unseen, and The Last Season. Fire of Love, Dosa’s documentary chronicling the work of Maurice and Katia Krafft, French husband-wife volcanologists, opened the Sundance Film Festival on January 20 this year. The film contains over 20 years of archival footage and dramatic shots of active volcanoes and explosions beginning in 1966. The Krafft couple traveled to volcanic locations in Zaire, Iceland, the Americas and Japan, capturing then-unseen footage of seismic, tectonic eruptions. Under her direction, the team behind Fire of Love weaved the Filmmaker Sara Dosa, a native Piedmotner. footage together to tell the couple’s love story - the Kraffts spent decades collecting data mere feet away from danger. In 1991 they were killed while filming an explosion on Japan’s Mount Unzen. In their wake, they left behind a legacy and some of the most dramatic footage humans may ever be able to capture. “I like to think of it as a love triangle. Maurice and Katia were obviously the love story that drove [the narrative], but you also have the volcanoes they chased. In a way, they were both in love with this important work they did,” Dosa said. The documentary recently was reviewed favorably in both the New York Times and San Francisco Chronicle. A.O Scott, co-chief film critic for the New York Times, noted the exceptional cinematography of the film. “The sheer existence of these photos is mind-boggling when you think about how close the people with the cameras must have been to the lava and the smoke,” said Scott. As director, Dosa had her hand in every stage of the film, including the documentary’s clever use of animation, and writing the copy provided to Miranda July, author and independent film screenwriter, who narrates the film. Dosa said she consulted with the Kraffts’ contemporaries and colleagues when considering what story she wanted to tell, but that the bulk of the narration comes directly from the footage the couple captured, and the Kraffts’ own notes, speeches and published works. National Geographic Films released Fire of Love on July 6 this month. Dosa’s documentary is currently showing at Alamo Drafthouse Cinema New Mission and AMC Kabuki 8 theatre in San Francisco. articles.text: A memorial soccer game in honor of Ralston Louie will be held at Witter Field this Friday, July 22 at 6:30 p.m. A member of the PHS Class of 2010, and honored then as the school’s Outstanding Male Athlete, he graduated from Williams College in Massachusetts in 2014 as cum laude, and was nearing graduating with s Master’s degree from the University of Southern California when he tragically passed away while swimming in Oakland on January 31, 2021. He was 28. A multi-sport athlete at PHS, he competed in football, soccer, and golf, and was a member of the soccer team in college. The memorial game on July 22 has been organized by his family, close friends and former teammates and former coach Fernando Romero It will be their second year of the memorial game. “I coached him when he was played for the Bay Oaks,” said Romero. “If you had 11 Ralstons, you’d win a World Cup. Ralston was special. Last year we got together on Father’s Day. A lot of the team lives outside the Bay Area but they still get together.” Romero described Louie as a “goalkeeper’s best friend” for his defensive prowess and had high praise for his demeanor and ability to learn as a player. Louie helped Bay Oaks reach the State Cup Finals. “He was the kind of kid you wanted as a coach. He was very coachable and at the same time, was able to give his opinion about what was working or what wasn’t,” said Romero. Playing in Friday’s game will be a collection of Louie’s former Bay Oaks and Piedmont High School teammates “Last year, we had about 15 players and are hoping to get 22 so I can referee,” said Romero with a laugh. Louie was a documentary filmmaker who was putting the finishing touches on a virtual reality project titled “Wing Wor,” which highlighted his return to his family’s ancestral village in China as part of the thesis for his Master’s degree from USC. Although Louie loved sports, his true passion was filmmaking. He created the Piedmont High film festival and recruited Pixar director Pete Docter as a judge. Ralston’s father, Reagan Louis, is a professor of Photography at San Francisco Art Institute. “As long as I’ve known him, I thought he was going to rule the world, he was a special guy. People are coming from the East Coast and different states to be here, so it says a lot about the person he was,” said Romero. His short film, “Roots & Branches,” was a semifinalist in the Youth Voices on China video contest in 2016. He was admitted to the master of fine arts program at the USC School of Cinematic Arts, where he later continued his athletic career on the school’s triathlon club and finished a half-triathlon in Southern California before the pandemic. “We’re so grateful to Fernando for putting this all together,” said Robin Wu, Ralston’s mother. “It’s just a scrimmage, but to have friends, family, and his sister who also played soccer get together is really special. pages.text: Wednesday, July 20, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. MAX COLE Rowing Piedmont High Class of 2022 St. Lawrence University Class of 2026 Max Cole recently graduated from Piedmont High and was part of a national title with Oakland Strokes on June 12 in Sarasota, Florida at the U.S. Rowing Youth National Championship Regatta. He was a member of the coxless quadruple scull that edged out the second place boat from Marina Aquatic Center of Los Angeles by just .6 of a second. The Youth National Championship attracts the best teams throughout the country with an estimated 3,500 student athletes from hundreds of teams throughout the U.S. in 34 separate races. Cole also competed with the Strokes at the prestigious Head of the Charles Regatta in October in Cambridge, Massachusetts as a member of the Varsity 8 boat. What is your workout program this summer? I’m focusing a lot on cardio fitness this summer. I’ll usually do one workout in the morning and one workout in the afternoon. In the morning, I do 80-90 minutes of cardio. My cardio is mostly on the rowing machine, but I’ll change it up with a bike ride or run twice a week. In afternoon sessions, I’ll focus more on strength. They’ll usually consist of a heavy lift, core, or hip strengthening. What are your fitness goals for this summer? I’m trying to prepare for the Fall season next year at college. Races will be six kilometers long, so my goal is to increase my VO2 max and be comfortable rowing for longer periods of time. How are you measuring your development? I usually measure my fitness with erg (ergometer) splits. I’ll record my erg splits after I erg, and I can compare them to previous erg splits. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’ll be working on my own this summer, but I’m still talking with my old coach about my training progress. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I won Youth National Championships in the Coxless 4 in early June. It was a big accomplishment that I’ve been working towards since my freshman year in high school. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Success in sports comes from the mindset. If you want to succeed, you need to have a goal in mind, and you need to know what needs to be done in order to achieve that goal. BRIT BURDEN Water Polo, Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2024 Brit Burden will be a junior at Piedmont High and is a two-sport athlete with water polo and basketball. He’s currently undertaking a busy summer playing on an AAU basketball team. Basketball coach Ben Spencer has praised Burden since last winter. He mentioned that Burden will give Piedmont considerable size (6 feet, 5 inches) and control of the boards, Burden earned an honorable mention for All-League honors as a sophomore. He had 10 points and seven rebounds in a 69-52 win over St. Joseph, scored 11 points in a narrow loss to O’Dowd, and 12 points in a 62-42 win over Berkeley. Brit Burden is entering his junior year at PHS and is a two-sport athlete with water polo in the fall and basketball in the winter. He’s set to be a starting forward on Ben Spencer’s basketball team. He was a starter on the water polo team last fall, helping them win its first WACC title in nearly 20 years. They finished the season at 19-6 and reached the NCS semifinals as the No. 3 seed. He scored twice in a 7-4 loss to No. 2 Marin Academy in the semi-finals. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program this summer is consistently working on my game in basketball through lifting, getting up shots with my teammates, practicing individually, and playing games in AAU. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals for this summer are to become more explosive as an athlete and build up my cardiovascular endurance. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development through tracking my lifts and seeing how my practice translates into game situations. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m working with my teammates, coaches, and by myself. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I have achieved is seeing the things I practice translate into game situations. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? You are the creator of your own reality. articles.text: New women’s team, Oakland Soul, to start in 2023 Oakland Roots SC, a professional men’s soccer team, is now 22 games into its season with 12 matches left on the docket. They are gearing up for a critical time to push for a playoff position in the USL Championship, the second year in the league for Roots. They are currently in ninth place, two out of the qualification zone. With 28 points, they are one point behind Sacramento Republic in seventh and two behind Los Angeles Galaxy II in sixth. Roots’ playing style can be described as possession based, with frequent overlapping runs from the outside. They are playing under 35-year old first-year head coach Juan Guerra, who was lured away from USL ChamOttar Magnus Karlsson, an Iceland native, is currently the league’s leader with 15 goals. Staff Photos Oakland Roots SC has 12 matches left in the season and is in the thick of a race for a final playoff spot. pion Phoenix Rising. The team has had strong performances, but has struggled with consistency, and currently sits with a record of six wins, 10 ties, and six losses. Oakland is coming off of a huge 4-0 victory over fifth-place El Paso Locomotive at Laney College on Saturday, July 16, where they scored all four goals before halftime. “We are performance oriented. Tonight, the result matched the performance. Many games this year, we’ve performed well and created a lot of chances but we didn’t have the opportunity to get the ball in the back of the net,” said Guerra following the victory over El Paso. Oakland currently has the league’s leading scorer, Ottar Magnus Karlsson, who has 15 goals. An Icelandic native, he is on loan from Italy’s Venezia—which plays in Serie B in Venice. Karlsson scored twice in the recent win over El Paso, but is not trying to focus on the Golden Boot race. “It doesn’t get too much into my head. I have my goals, my vision, so I just try to keep grounded and focused on the rest of the season. And then, yeah, we can talk,” said Karlsson. Roots will host eighth-place Las Vegas in a pivotal game this Saturday, July 23. They’ll have a short week of rest with another game at Laney on Wednesday, July 27 against 11th place Phoenix before starting a two-week break until August 13 at Detroit City. Photo courtesy of USL W League Oakland Soul is the Roots’ women’s team, slated for its inaugural season in 2023 in the USL Women’s League. Women’s team to start in 2023 The Roots’ women’s team, Oakland Soul, was announced on Tuesday, May 24 and is slated to start its first season in 2023 in the USL Women’s League, considered the “pre-professional” development stage. The team will offer players a chance to train at their top-of-the-line training center at the former Oakland Raiders facility on Bay Farm Island in Alameda, while they play their games at Merritt College on their inaugural season. The W League will be considered Division 3 in the hierarchy of U.S. soccer. The USL Super League, also scheduled for 2023-2024, is listed as Division 2 behind the top-tier NWSL. An NWSL constituent is being planned for San Jose in the future, but they are still in the works of determining a name. Soul’s mission will be to attract younger soccer stars in the Bay Area away from some of the top competitive regional soccer clubs. It’s unclear what type of contract the Soul will be able to offer athletes, but one former NWSL player told me that they have reached out to her—which tells me they may be able to attract some players with professional experience. Jonas Vingegaard of Jumbo-Visma overtook Tadej Pogačar for the Yellow Jersey on Stage 11’s mountain ride from Albertville to Col du Granon Serre Chevalier, building a 2 minute and 22 second lead over the Slovenian. The race now heads into the Pyrenees mountains for Stage 17 and 18. Pogačar faded badly in Stage 11 on the final climb on the Col du Granon. With 3.5 kilometers to go, Vingegaard and his team attacked for the stage win. It was shocking to see Pogačar crack. He had seemed destined to win the race again this year. Since then Vingegaard, a Dane, has thwarted continuous attacks from Pogačar. What’s becoming evident is the superior team in Jumbo-Visma compared to Pogačar’s UAE Emirates squad. Vingegaard has strong support around him, while Pogacar appears to be isolated. Pogačar attacked at the last kilometer of Stage 12’s mountain ride from Briançon to Alpe d’Huez Tadej, but Vingegaard effectively matched him with each sprint, including a break to the finish line. The same held true in Stage 16. Vingegaard held off several attacks by Pogačar by responding each time the Slovenian broke into a sprint. What’s becoming clear is that Vingegaard has the legs to keep up and a team with fellow Jumbo-Visma rider Sepp Kuss keeping a strong pace at the front of the pack. Now the Grand Tour moves into its final two mountain stages on 17 and 18, which could be the final opportunity for Pogačar to regain the Yellow Jersey and a critical time for Vingegaard to ultimately secure the lead in General Classification. articles.text: The Washburn Fire that threatened a historic grove of sequoia trees in Yosemite National Park has now been fully contained at Yosemite’s Mariposa Grove. Residents were allowed to return to the Wawona community on Sunday, July 17. The fire is 58 percent contained at 4,863 acres after having consumed 3,221 acres last week. The fire has been burning since July 7. Yosemite West remains accessible from the northern side of Wawona road with Mariposa Grove closed until further notice. The Wawona community and Mariposa Grove are still closed to the public. Last week fire crews installed a sprinkler system to help prevent the blaze spread into the historic Mariposa Grove of 500 sequoias, including the 3,000- year old “Grizzly Giant.” The giant sequoias avoided damage due to the work from fire crews. In addition, prescribed burns over the last several years also helped limit harm to the area. “This part of the grove is in pretty good shape,” said Yosemite National Park Forest Ecologist Garrett Dickman. “We got low flame lengths over here and it’s just cleaning the things up; it looks like a nice clean burn. There are other parts of the fire that are of more concern, but I think the grove will be in good shape. We have decades of prescribed fire in here and I think that’s what’s going to save these big trees.” On July 15, the U.S. Forest Service announced that the nearby Sierra National Forest will have portions closed due to the Washburn Fire breaching into an area in a “difficult to access” region along the Merced River. “The Washburn Fire is now on the Sierra National Forest. The Fire is moving east along the South Fork of Merced River in a remote river canyon making it difficult to access. The Fire is impacting wilderness and main forest roads and areas of recreation. This will call for significant firefighting and forest resources to help fight the advancing progress of the Washburn Fire. For these reasons, the impacted areas and roads will need to be closed for the safety of public visitors and fire personnel,” stated the U.S. Forest Service. Photo courtesy of the Associated Press The Washburn Fire no longer threatens the historic sequoia trees in the Mariposa Grove at Yosemite National Park. The full incident is at 58 percent containment, but has breached into the Sierra National Forest.

articles.text: Diego Rivera’s enormous mural, “Pan American Unity”, will be on display at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art through next summer, 2023. On June 17, 2021, Diego Rivera’s colossal fresco “Pan American Unity” was carefully moved from San Francisco’s City College to SF MOMA. The priceless 4,000 pound panel, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster is 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 steel-framed panels bolted together and weighing about 21 tons. It was designed to be portable and was moved to the college campus from Treasure Island after its completion. It is the largest of the artist’s works and completely spanned the narrow lobby of the college’s theater, now named Diego Rivera Theater. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, where it officially went on display in June 2021. In partnership with City College, SFMOMA will display “Pan American Unity” in the museum free to the public until 2023, when it will then return to City College to be installed in a new performing arts center. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pan-american-unity/ to learn more.
articles.title: Diego Rivera’s massive “Pan American Unity” now at SFMOMA

I’m not sure if we are on the other side of the tenacious, ever-changing Covid-19 pandemic, but by all appearances – maskless travelers in airports, diners in restaurants, shoppers in stores – it seems Americans have decided we are. But I am sure this virus has wrought change in countless ways that we are just beginning to understand. What comes to mind here is the question of will we ever watch movies as we did in, say, 2019, with walk-in theaters and blockbuster weekends. Will the filmmaking industry ever be the same? I recently read an article in the New York Times by Nicole Sperling, titled “The Last Movie Star.” She was writing about Tom Cruise and the recently released Top Gun: Maverick, which begins with the now iconic, adrenalin-pumping song “Highway to the Danger Zone” by Harold Faltermeyer. Sperling’s thesis is that after the last two plus years of quarantines and business shutdowns, the film-going audience has changed as have their options regarding movie watching. Massive home entertainment centers, streaming platforms such as Netflix have increased, plus the absence of large groups of people sitting shoulder-to-shoulder in movie theaters during a pandemic. In other words, those halcyon days of Hollywood red carpet glamor and lavish releases of major films seem to be a thing of the past, as are those times when there were actors known as “movie stars.” Sperling argues that Tom Cruise is the last true movie star. He is that performer who can draw audiences to his film, not because of its compelling story, but rather simply because of his “star” persona. He is more than just an actor who speaks those emotive lines written by someone else; rather, he has long ago transcended the character he portrays (the role seems almost incidental), and does so in a medium that is, to be sure, larger than life. So, the question begged is does it matter today who wears the tights or the cape or who is the character suffering from a climactic sense of angst? Not really. But in the case of Cruise, it does. And that is what the Top Gun: Maverick studio is counting on. Cruise will pull back into the theater those over-40 viewers who remember the thrill of watching Maverick lifting off that aircraft carrier to confront an unnamed adversary. And then there’s the fact that Cruise has made 44 films, earning $4.4 billion in the U.S, and Canada alone. A stunning achievement. But there is the reality that this summer he turned 60. Who will or can possibly follow? Or is he indeed “The Last Movie Star”?

articles.text: The Gentlemen, written and directed by Guy Ritchie, is a stylized caper-comedy. It’s a blend of 50s noir, gangsta Goodfellas, and Tarantino-like dialogue, full of surprises, all while sustaining its cool-to-the-end street cred. The film opens with two men sitting by a fireplace late at night sipping expensive scotch: one is Ray (Charlie Hunnam), the righthand man of Michael Pearson (Matthew McConaughey), an American ex-pat and British drug kingpin (weed only). Across from him is Fletcher (Hugh Grant), a journalist, who has meticulously, he thinks, put together surveillance notes and photos, a kind of dossier, his mission being to blackmail Pearson using Ray as the go-between. Fletcher begins his pitch, asking Ray if he might tell him a story. When Ray reluctantly agrees, the plot begins, told like a movie in flashbacks, flash forwards, freeze frames, while establishing that sleazy Fletch is an unreliable narrator. Fletcher reveals that he knows that Pearson is looking to sell his entire marijuana operation to include processing and delivery. Apparently, he grows his weed at multiple locations, meaning lands owned by English gentry who need the cash flow to maintain their estates and titled lifestyles. Word has gotten out that Pearson has a wealthy buyer and they are in negotiations ($400 million pounds); however, a bidding war (literally) has been set in motion, meaning some very bad people (an Asian gang) are going to get wacked, possible Pearson himself. There is also some betrayal in the works; it’s hinted that Pearson and Ray are not completely in the dark about what is afoot. Fletcher’s offer to Ray is in order to buy his silence regarding all that has thus far transpired (we’re back in real time) it will cost Pearson and his much-loved wife, Rosalind (Michelle Dockery), a steely partner in crime, $20 million pounds. He points out that that is but a fraction of the multiple millions he knows is generate each year by the grow farms. A few bags of thousand-pound notes and he walks away. It’s impossible to capture the twists, turns and double-crosses that take place. Better to see it all in multiple reveals. But know that it’s enjoyable. The cast is superb, led by McConaughey doing his insouciant best to swagger while remaining a gangster in a tux who socializes with sophisticates. Colin Farrell drops in for a cameo that is wonderful, portraying a boxing coach whose boys all work out at his gym, a group standing ready to do whatever is necessary for the team and the boss. It’s a fun crew – deadly but amusing in their jarring plaid workout gear. Pay attention, especially during the third act, which is piled up with stuff to be explained, along with more than a few loose ends to be tied off. The Gentlemen. Written and directed by Guy Ritchie. Starring Matthew McConaughey, Charlie Hunnam and Hugh Grant. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated R. Released into theaters and reviewed in the Post in 2020. Now streaming on Prime/Netflix/VUDU/ A scene for Guy Ritchie’s movie, The Gentlemen.

articles.text: Consider Ice Age, a computer-animated family fun prologue to an entertaining franchise. This debut introduces odd-couple characters such as grumpy Manfred, a wooly mammoth (Ray Romano), Sid the snoring sloth (John Leguizamo), and sneaky Diego, a saber-toothed tiger. The story takes place some 20,000 years ago when the earth was a wondrous, pristine, prehistoric place. It is called the Pleistocene period. It was also a time filled with a bevy of now extinct animals, and the beginning of what is known as the Ice Age. As the planet began to cool, most of those animals migrated south to warmer climes, all except for Manny, a wooly mammoth, and Sid, an ever clumsy and annoying sloth. The odd couple decide to head north, and thus begins their adventure into a landscape of massive white glaciers and waterways that are slowly freezing over. Before long the pair unexpectedly come across a human mother trying to save her baby from a freezing lake. Just before she drowns in the attempt, she asks Manny and Sid to bring her baby, called Roshan, back to its tribe. The two agree. It’s at this point they encounter a saber-toothed tiger named Diego (Denis Leary) who volunteers to be their tracker as they search for little Roshan’s family. What Manny and Sid don’t realize is that Diego has his own nefarious reasons for joining the trio, reasons that have to do with his own pack of tigers and the fate of Roshan. Along the way, the trio plus one encounter numerous obstacles and unanticipated misadventures. It’s in this first tale that the audience is introduced to Scrat (Chris Wedge), a monomaniacal squirrel-rat who has only one mission, and that’s to get his paws on a particular acorn and bury it for what will be a long winter. Scrat is a wonderful Looney Toon character who appears only intermittently during the narrative, and soon becomes a running gag. This charming critter, ever bugeyed, never speaks; instead, it just squeaks and screeches while chasing the elusive nut. The little rodent becomes a scene-stealer, always hilariously funny, akin to the Road Runner. Ice Age is sprightly, has lots of laugh-out-loud dialogue, and proves to be delightful, wholesome entertainment. Ice Age. Animated comedy-adventure directed by Chris Hedge. With the voices of Ray Romano, John Legouizamo, and Denis Leary. 1 hr., 21 min. Rated PG. Released in 2002. Now Streaming on Disney+/Prime/Vudu. articles.text: Meet the Robinsons was released by Disney in 2007 and is loosely based on a children’s book written by William Joyce. It is a futuristic fantasy and constantly tweaks time travel. The story begins in the present where we see a desperate mother leaving her baby at the doorstep of an orphanage. Years pass, and the baby, now called Lewis (Daniel Hansen), has grown into a bright, hard-working, 12-year-old inventor with big round glasses and wheat-colored hair, who creates marvelous things. An example of one of his gadgets is a brain scanner, created by Lewis with the hope that he can scan his memory and discover who his biological parents are. Unfortunately, some of his inventions have a tendency to blow up, including when potential adoptive parents come to the orphanage looking for a child. Lewis, they conclude, is just too strange to take home. At this point in the story the plot makes a dramatic shift. Lewis, determined to find his family, the Robinsons, makes the decision to leave his roommate, Goober (Matthew Josten), and the orphanage in search of his mother. But before he can launch his plan he meets Wilbur Andersen (Wesley Singerman), a smooth-talking newbie teen who happens to possess a time machine. Of course, Lewis is more than fascinated. A time machine, if it actually works, just might help him find his mom. And work it does. Lewis is transported 25 years into the future by Wilbur, and thus begins the film’s real adventure when suddenly Lewis finds himself in an entirely new dimension. To his delight, Lewis does find his family, the Robinsons, and discovers that they are also inventors in this futuristic era, a time so strange that even a Tyrannosaurus appears, apparently from the very distant past. Naturally, there is some action (a chase scene with a T.rex), and lots of gags involving time travel and wonderful inventions. But the story’s emotional center, from the outset, is Lewis, who is sadly convinced that he doesn’t belong anywhere. He has always wondered why he was abandoned as a baby, and longs to discover the answer. What makes the film continually interesting is the contrast between the Lewis’ present and that world 25 years in the future. Hint: keep an eye out for the guy in a bowler hat (Stephen Anderson). Meet the Robinsons. Animate d a d ve nt u re - c ome d y directed by Stephen J. Anderson. With the voices of Angela Basset, Daniel Hansen, and Tom Selleck. 1 hr.,34 min. Rated G. Released in 2007. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+. A scene from Disney’s Meet the Robinsons.
articles.title: Meet the Robinsons a sweet story of time travel

articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight will be performed by San Francisco Ballet at Stanford on August 5. San Francisco Ballet will return with two live performances on August 5 and 6. The company will perform a program of three short ballets outside at Stanford University’s Frost Amphitheater. The program includes Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight, Jerome Robbin’s In the Night, and William Forsythe’s Blake Works I. The short ballets range greatly in theme and choreography, with music by Bach, Chopin and James Blake. Both performances will begin at 8 p.m. Frost Amphitheater is located on the Stanford University campus at 351 Lassen Street in Palo Alto. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sf ballet.org/ calendar/starry-nights-at-stanford-live/. Students of the AileyCamp dance program will perform their final showcase on July 28.

articles.text: AileyCamp, a full-scholarship program that promotes personal development through dance for middle school students from the East Bay, will perform on-stage at Zellerbach Hall on July 28. The event is offered free of charge through Cal Performances. The student program’s final showcase performance, “Believing We Can,” is inspired by a theme of faith. Dancers will be supported with professional staging, lighting and costumes and will perform with live music. “AileyCamp supports one of Cal Performances’ key goals of ensuring that everyone can feel connected to the performing arts. Performance is a means by which we can learn about ourselves and about the world around us, and, as we know from experiences with AileyCamp over these past 20 years, this ability to foster growth and empathy can be transformative at an often-tumultuous time in young people’s lives,” said Jeremy Geffen, Executive and Artistic Director of Cal Performances. “Having run AileyCamp for 20 years, we now have the privilege of seeing not just the immediate impact, but also the ways AileyCamp has shaped campers’ lives well into adulthood – including some who have felt so empowered by the program that they’ve returned to serve as leaders for the next generation of campers.” Patricia West serves as Director for the performance. She describes AileyCamp as a transformative experience for students. “It inspires youth to be their best selves with a curriculum that encompasses dance, storytelling, and both personal and professional life skills. AileyCamp is a supportive environment where campers leave feeling empowered and engaged in the world around them,” she said. “Our team of instructors and administrators, many of whom are professional artists in their own right, are dedicated to every camper’s success. Reflecting on the past 20 years, it is my hope that Berkeley/Oakland AileyCamp continues to have a meaningful impact by helping youth thrive academically, socially, and emotionally.” The showcase begins at 7 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus on Bancroft Way. More details about AileyCamp can be found on Cal Performances’ website at calperformances.org/aileycamp. Donations in support of AileyCamp for its 20th anniversary are welcomed at calperformances.org/aileycamp-20.

The group crossed Wildwood Avenue and walked through the Hall Fenway. The trains once ran here too. The fenway has been beautifully landscaped and maintained by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation since 1964. It was easy to imagine streetcars rolling through this spot on their way to the end of the line at what is now Crocker Park. It was reported that the home just above the fenway, on the corner of Wildwood and Crocker, was the site of a stationhouse for the streetcar line. The walkers crossed Crocker Avenue and went on Hampton Road past Crocker Park. This park is also known as “Bear Park” because of the Benny Bufano granite sculpture of a mother bear and her twin cubs in the park’s center. The group walked up Hampton to the landscaped triangle at the corner with Indian Road. It believed this is the location of the trains’ turnaround and overnight parking spot. The group turned down Indian to an interesting, short section of road between the upper and lower portions of LaSalle Avenue. This short part of the street is only about 100 feet long, but few people realize it actually bisects LaSalle before LaSalle continues on to the southern portion of Crocker Avenue, while Indian Road continues on to the Oakland/Piedmont city border. The walkers had a fun discussion about whether this section of road is LaSalle Avenue or Indian Road. The walkers went to the corner where LaSalle clearly resumes and followed it to Crocker. articles.text: INGREDIENTS Every summer we are gifted with a generous quantity of plums from our neighbors’ tree. It was planted by previous owners, so we’re not sure of the variety. We only know the tree is older and the plums are abundant, delicious, and juicy! So for a couple of weeks every summer I like to add plums to everything, including salads. This recipe came about when I had a craving for a taste of Southeast Asia. I was thinking of making skewers of chicken and pork satay on the barbeque and mixing up a spicy peanut sauce for dipping. Then I decided the same flavors would make for a great salad too. I encourage mixing and matching with vegetables you enjoy. I purposefully left the list of salad ingredients on the sparse side for my presentation, which can be composed or tossed altogether depending on your serving situation. Add cooked, shredded, or sliced chicken or pork for a heartier option. If I prepare anything with nuts, especially peanuts, I make sure it’s obvious to anyone who may have allergies to nuts and allow them to pass on this dish. The peanut butter in the dressing isn’t obvious upon serving, so the garnish of chopped peanuts on top signals its presence. An advance note: This recipe calls for unseasoned rice vinegar. Next to it on your grocer’s shelf you may also find seasoned rice vinegar. There is a big difference between the two. “Seasoned” rice vinegar includes salt, sugar and sometimes MSG. I prefer only getting the unseasoned option, only rice and water, then choosing how I add flavor. Piedmont Plum Salad with Spicy Peanut Dressing Makes 3–4 servings, depending on appetites For the dressing: • 1/4 cup unseasoned, rice wine vinegar • 1 tablespoon peanut butter, room temperature if refrigerated • 1 - 2 teaspoons sambal oelek, substitute any Asian chili-garlic paste or sriracha sauce, to taste • 1 tablespoon neutral-flavored oil • 1 teaspoon toasted sesame seed oil • 1/2 - 1 teaspoon fish sauce, substitute with 1 - 2 teaspoons soy sauce, to taste • 1/4 teaspoon ground white pepper For the salad: • 4 cups crisp salad greens such as Romain lettuce, Little Gems, napa cabbage, etc. • 1-1/2 cup of plums, about 4 plums pitted and sliced into half-inch wedges • 1 cup cucumber, thinly sliced • 1/2 cup radishes, thinly sliced • 1/4 cup shallots, thinly sliced. Substitute red onion or the whites of green onion • 2 Tablespoons dry-roasted peanuts, roughly chopped INSTRUCTIONS Making the dressing: In a small bowl combine the dressing ingredients and whisk until smooth and emulsified. Taste to adjust for acidity, spicy-heat level, and saltiness. Thin with a bit of water if necessary to reach a thick, creamy texture (similar to ranch or green goddess dressings). Making the salad: Prepare the leafy greens of choice. Select crispy, crunchy varieties that will hold up to the creamy dressing. Serve as a composed salad with the ingredients separated and the dressing drizzled atop or toss all of the salad ingredients together with the dressing mixed throughout. Garnish with chopped peanuts.

articles.text: The hot, dry Piedmont summer is upon us. Beat the heat and avoid any unexpected home snafus by following these simple tips. Tip 1: Turn your AC on before it gets too hot in the day Air conditioning is only designed to cool rooms about 20 degrees below current temps. A good rule of thumb to keep your system from working too hard? Flip the “on” switch when temperatures get to around 80 degrees and are expected to climb higher. And don’t forget to check that your filters are free of buildup — when they clog, air flow is blocked and costs quickly go up. Tip 2: Add weatherstripping to keep the cool air in and costs lower Weatherstrip around windows and doors every 1-2 years to close gaps that let cool air escape. If you’re using self-adhesive tape, make sure you’re applying it to a clean surface. Properly applied, weatherstripping can save around 10% on year-round energy usage, according to the Environmental Protection Agency’s ENERGY Clean gutters of winter debris to stave off water damage. If you notice your water usage increasing more than usual, you may be losing precious H2O through a hard-to-find leak in your irrigation system. articles.text: When many people hear the words “estate planning,” they assume it’s just for the wealthy. But that’s not the case because everyone can benefit from an estate plan. And when you’re creating one, you’ll want to avoid some common mistakes. Before we look at those mistakes, let’s go over what estate planning is designed to accomplish. Essentially, an estate plan allows you to pass on your assets in the way you desire. But it can also specify other actions, such as naming someone to care for your minor children if you were no longer around. In creating an estate plan, several key documents are involved, including a will, a trust, a financial power of attorney and a medical power of attorney or a health care directive. Now, let’s consider a few estate-planning mistakes: • Not communicating your plans You’ll need to inform your family about whom you’ve chosen as executor – the individual who will administer your estate – and whom you’ve named as the trustee – the person who will manage your trust’s assets. (You can also choose a trust company to handle this duty.) And to help avoid unpleasant surprises when your estate is being settled, consider letting your children or other close relatives know who will be receiving what. • Not reviewing your plans periodically Once you create your estate plans, don’t forget about them. Over time, your personal situation may change – you may experience a remarriage or bring in new children. Your interests may change, too – perhaps you’ll become deeply involved in supporting a favorite charitable organization. Given these and other potential changes, you’ll want to review your estate plans once in a while to see if they need to be modified. • Not updating beneficiary designations Every so often, you may want to review the beneficiary designations on your life insurance policies, investment accounts and retirement assets. As mentioned, changes in your life, such as remarriage and the addition of new children, may affect your beneficiaries. Beneficiary designations are powerful and can even supersede your will, so you’ll want to update them as needed. Also, if you have a 529 education savings plan, you’ll want to name a successor owner – someone who can take over your 529 if you were to pass away. • Not re-registering assets placed in a trust A living trust offers you many potential benefits, such as the ability to bypass the time-consuming and highly public process of probate when it’s time to settle your estate. However, just establishing the trust, by itself, may be insufficient – you likely also need to re-register assets, such as your investments, so they are officially owned by the trust, not by you. This is essential for the trust to work as you intended. Here’s one other mistake. Not getting the help you need. Estate planning can be complex, so you’ll want to work with an attorney, and possibly with your financial advisor and tax professional, too. By avoiding key mistakes and working with a qualified team of professionals, you can create and maintain an estate plan that will help you leave the legacy you desire. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, July 20, 2022 Summer’s here: Tips for keeping your house in top shape The hot, dry Piedmont summer is upon us. Beat the heat and avoid any unexpected home snafus by following these simple tips. Tip 1: Turn your AC on before it gets too hot in the day Air conditioning is only designed to cool rooms about 20 degrees below current temps. A good rule of thumb to keep your system from working too hard? Flip the “on” switch when temperatures get to around 80 degrees and are expected to climb higher. And don’t forget to check that your filters are free of buildup — when they clog, air flow is blocked and costs quickly go up. Tip 2: Add weatherstripping to keep the cool air in and costs lower Weatherstrip around windows and doors every 1-2 years to close gaps that let cool air escape. If you’re using self-adhesive tape, make sure you’re applying it to a clean surface. Properly applied, weatherstripping can save around 10% on year-round energy usage, according to the Environmental Protection Agency’s ENERGY Clean gutters of winter debris to stave off water damage. Turn your AC on—before it gets too hot in the day. STAR program. Tip 3: Clean gutters of winter debris to stave off water damage Gutters divert water off your roof and help stave off potential leaks. Use these balmy, dry months of the Piedmont summer to remove debris that might have accumulated in the spring, and be sure to finish the job before the rainy season resumes in the fall. If you notice your water usage increasing more than usual, you may be losing precious H2O through a hard-to-find leak in your irrigation system. A water sensor like Flume or Flo can easily detect spikes in usage and will alert you instantly. Also be on the lookout for dripping hose bibs that may need replacing. Tip 4: Curb unnecessary water usage with one simple tool Tip 5: Avoid these summer gotchas when you’re out of town Set your hot water heater to vacation mode to keep your bills lower and turn off the gas pilot light to avoid a potential leak. articles.text: Dress Best for Less hosts a bag sale on the last Saturday of every month from 10 a.m. to noon at its Marking Room at 799 Magnolia Avenue. For $10 you can fill a paper grocery bag with items like clothing, toys, books, and bric-abrac items. Dress Best for Less (DBFL) was founded in 1982 by Piedmont resident Wendy Willrich and a group of Haven’s School moms, who decided to collect unneeded household items and clothing to sell to the community to raise money for the school district. They were given an unused room at Haven’s School, but quickly outgrew the space and rented a storefront on Piedmont Avenue, their original location. DBFL donates most of its profits to the Piedmont Education Foundation, a non-profit that is devoted to promoting academic excellence, investing in innovation and sustained financial support to the Piedmont Unified School District. Over one million dollars has been donated since the store’s inception.Donations that cannot be sold in the store are donated to other organizations. The store gives back to the broader community by donating to St. Vincent de Paul, Children’s Hospital, and animal rescue organizations in the East Bay. More than half of clothing donations received by DBFL are donated to St. Vincent de Paul, helping families in need in Alameda County through gifts made directly to them or through proceeds made from the store. These proceeds allow the organization to provide food, rent, job training and other services to those in need. DBFL also donates children’s items to Love Twice, a non-profit organization that provides newborns in need with quality baby clothing for the first year of life. Donations of gently used, high quality clothing and home goods are welcome, and all donations are tax deductible. The retail store is next to Piedmont Grocery at 4020 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. Store hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. DBFL’s marking room for sales and donations is by appointment only. Visit http://dressbestforless.org/donate/ to make an appointment. Personally, my home value is my entire life’s equity, which I have to live on the rest of my life. I have no pension, virtually no income, and my small art business has lost money the last several years. Thus, if a small faction changes Piedmont’s laws and regulations and character and home values, I will be forced to initiate or join a Class Action lawsuit in order to live out my life on my only equity: my Piedmont home.
